In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-'Adiyat

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By the racers, panting,﴾ ﴿And those that strike sparks of fire,﴾ ﴿And those that attack at dawn,﴾ ﴿And raise thereby dust,﴾ ﴿And penetrate thereby into the midst of a gathering.﴾

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him in his dictation, said:

Al-'Adiyat is the plural of 'adiyah, and al-'adiyat are those that run swiftly in their course.

So the meaning of al-'Adiyat is: He swears by those that run swiftly in their course.

Then he said: Most of the scholars hold that what is meant is horses, running in battle, and the purpose is to magnify the matter of jihad in the way of Allah.

Some scholars said: What is meant by al-'Adiyat is camels that run with the pilgrims from 'Arafat to Muzdalifah and Mina.

As for the meaning of His saying, ḍabḥan (panting): that they pant with a panting sound. It is a absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and al-ḍabḥ (panting) is the sound of the insides of horses when they run.

This supports the first view, which says they are camels, since panting is not exclusive to horses.

﴿Fa-l-muriyati qadḥan (And those that strike sparks of fire)﴾: that is, horses strike fire from stones with their hooves when they travel at night.

Likewise, the one who said al-'Adiyat are camels said: by their raising the stones, so some of them strike others.

And this meaning is supported by the poet's saying:

Her two forelegs drive away the pebbles at every midday heat, like the driving away of dirhams by money-changers.

(p-٦٢) ﴿Fa-l-mughirati ṣubḥan (And those that attack at dawn)﴾: horses raid the enemy at the time of dawn.

According to the second view: camels raid with the pilgrims at dawn from Muzdalifah to Mina on the day of sacrifice.

﴿Fa-atharna bihi naq'an (And raise thereby dust)﴾: that is, dust. He said "bihi": that is, with the dawn, or "bihi": that is, with the enemy.

What is understood from al-'Adiyat: they penetrate thereby into the midst of a gathering, that is, they enter into the midst of a gathering, that is, a great multitude of disbelievers.

A parallel of this meaning is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Hazim:

So they penetrated their host, and the one who hides escaped beneath the dust-cloud in the dark dust.

And according to the second view, which says: al-'Adiyat are camels carrying the pilgrims.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿Fa-wasatna bihi jam'an (and penetrate thereby into the midst of a gathering)﴾, that is: they became, by reason of that enemy, in the midst of a gathering. This is Muzdalifah, and jam' is one of the names of Muzdalifah.

This meaning is supported by the saying of Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, aunt of the Prophet (ﷺ) and mother of al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, may Allah be pleased with them both:

By the racers, dust-raising in the gathering, in their hands, when the dust rises, no!

This which the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, cited, has gathered the sayings of all the exegetes on these verses, and I have transmitted it in its own words to clarify the meaning completely.

However, among what he put forward, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, is that among the kinds of clarification in al-Adwa': when the scholars of exegesis differ regarding a meaning, and the verse contains an indication that rejects one of the two sayings or supports one of them, he points to it.

I have found that the exegetes differ regarding these verses on a fundamental point, while agreeing on the words, their meanings, and their style and structure.

The point of disagreement is the meaning of the "gathering" (jam') into which they penetrated: is it Muzdalifah, since among its names is Jam', as in the hadith: "I stood here, and all of Jam' is a place of standing"?

This is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in a discussion between him and Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Jarir related it.

(p-٦٣) Or is it the gathering of the army in battle, as previously mentioned, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and others. Ibn Jarir and others related it.

We have found numerous indications in the verse that prevent the intended meaning from being Muzdalifah as "jam'", and they are as follows: First, the describing of horses or camels alike with al-'Adiyat, to the extent of the panting, the striking of fire with hooves and pebbles, because these are attributes that indicate swift running.

It is known that the outpouring from 'Arafat and then from Muzdalifah does not bear this running, and it is not praiseworthy in it, for the Prophet (ﷺ) used to call out: "Tranquility, tranquility!" So if it had existed, it would not have been a place of magnification and exaltation.

Second: that it is well known that raising dust is among the requirements of war, as Bashshar said:

As if the source of the dust-cloud above our heads, and our swords, were a night whose stars are falling.

That is, because of the intensity of the charging and retreating.

Third: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Fa-l-mughirati ṣubḥan﴾ ﴿Fa-atharna bihi naq'an﴾ ﴿Fa-wasatna bihi jam'an﴾ came arranged with "fa", which indicates sequence and immediacy.

The raiding at dawn has been mentioned, and after it: "they penetrated thereby into a gathering."

Jam' is Muzdalifah, and one only goes there at night. How then would the raiding at dawn be paired with penetrating Muzdalifah at night?

And according to what the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, reported, that they raid at dawn from Muzdalifah to Mina, that raid would be at dawn after penetrating a jam', and the context places it after the raid, not before it.

Thus it has become clear that the intended meaning of Muzdalifah is not attainable in this context.

The other view remains, and it is the more correct. And Allah knows best.

If we returned to the theory of the interconnection of the surahs, it would favour this meaning: that in the preceding surah, the earthquake was mentioned, and the people's departure in scattered groups to be shown their deeds.

(p-٦٤) Here He urges the best deeds, which bequeath eternal life and lasting happiness, in a similar form: their running in scattered groups in the way of Allah to achieve that deed which they love to see at that time, which is supporting the religion of Allah or martyrdom in the way of Allah. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 100, verse 6:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ ﴿and indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ ﴿and indeed he is, in his love of wealth, intense﴾.

This is the answer. Al-Qurtubi said: *al-kanud* (the ungrateful one) is *al-kafur al-juhud li-ni'am Allah* (the one who is deeply ungrateful for the blessings of God), and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Hasan said: "He mentions the calamities and forgets the blessings." A poet took this and versified it:

*O you who are unjust in your conduct, while injustice is returned upon the one who committed it,*
*How long will you be, and until when, complaining of misfortunes and forgetting blessings?*

Abu Umamah al-Bahili narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "*Al-kanud* is the one who eats alone, withholds his gift, and beats his servant."

Ibn 'Abbas narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not inform you about the worst of you?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "The one who dwells alone, withholds his gift, and whips his servant." Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim recorded both in *Nawadir al-Usul*.

Ibn 'Abbas also narrated that he said: "*Al-kanud* in the language of Kindah and Hadramawt means the disobedient; in the language of Rabi'ah and Mudar, the ungrateful; and in the language of Kinanah, the miser with bad character."

Muqatil said, and the poet said:

*Ungrateful toward the favors of men; and whoever is ungrateful toward the favors of men is distanced.*

That is: ungrateful.

Then it was said: he is the one who disbelieves in the little and does not give thanks for the much.

It was also said: he is the one who denies the truth.

It was also said: Kindah was named Kindah because it denied (*jahadat*) its father.

Ibrahim ibn Harmah the poet said:

*Leave the misers, if they become arrogant and turn away; and the mention of the miserliness of Thamaniyah is ungrateful.*

[This is] in many transmissions and evidences.

Among the meanings: *al-kanud* is the one who spends the blessings of Allah in disobedience to Allah.

And from Dhu al-Nun: *al-halu'* and *al-kanud* are: the one who, when evil touches him, is distressed, and when good touches him, withholds.

It was also said: *al-hasud al-haqud* (the envious and rancorous one).

Then al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said at the end of the discussion:

I say: all these sayings return to the meaning of ingratitude and denial.

The Prophet ﷺ explained the meaning of *al-kanud* by blameworthy traits and non-praiseworthy states. If this is authentic, it is the highest of what is said, and no one has any further statement with it. End of quotation.

Thus, as he said: if the report is authentic, there is no saying for anyone. However, all these attributes fall under the category of *ikhtilaf al-tanawwu'* (variation of diversity, where differing expressions describe the same reality), because they are included within the meaning of denying the truth or the blessings.

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri used the noble verse as evidence, and it explains *al-kanud* according to the earlier meanings, that he is *al-halu'* ﴿when evil touches him, distressed﴾ ﴿and when good touches him, withholding﴾.

Similar to it is His saying: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him, honoring him and bestowing favor upon him, he says, "My Lord has honored me." But when He tests him, restricting his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ [Al-Fajr: 15-16].

He also commented there with the same as he commented here.

There, He said: ﴿No! Rather, you do not honor the orphan﴾ ﴿and do not encourage one another to feed the needy﴾ ﴿and you devour inheritance, consuming it altogether﴾ ﴿and you love wealth with immense love﴾ [Al-Fajr: 17-20].

Here, He commented on it with His saying: ﴿and indeed he is, in his love of wealth, intense﴾. And Allah knows best.

His saying "Indeed, mankind" is general, encompassing every human being, and it is known that some humans are not like this, (p-66) as He said: ﴿As for he who gives and fears Allah﴾ ﴿and believes in the best reward﴾ [Al-Layl: 5-6], which indicates that it is of the *al-'amm al-makhsus* (general term qualified by specification).

And these attributes are part of human nature except what the Shari'ah refines, as He said: ﴿And souls have been present with stinginess﴾ [An-Nisa': 128],

and His saying: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, those are the successful﴾ [Al-Hashr: 9].

The Shaykh stated in his dictation that the intended meaning of it is the disbeliever.

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab*:

(p-462) In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah al-'Adiyat.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ ﴿and indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ and so on.

This verse indicates that man is a witness against the ingratitude of his own soul, meaning his extremity in disbelief.

Other verses have come that indicate otherwise:

• Like His saying: ﴿And they think that they are doing good work﴾ [Al-Kahf: 104],

• and His saying: ﴿And they think that they are guided﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 37],

• and His saying: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not expected﴾ [Az-Zumar: 47].

The answer to this is from three aspects:

The first: that man's testimony that he is ungrateful is the testimony of his state by the manifestation of his ingratitude, and the state sometimes suffices in place of speech.

The second: that his testimony against himself with that will be on the Day of Resurrection, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And they will testify against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ [Al-An'am: 130], and His saying: ﴿So they will acknowledge their sin. So away with the companions of the Blaze﴾ [Al-Mulk: 11], and His saying: ﴿They will say, "Yes, but the word of punishment has come into effect upon the disbelievers"﴾ [Az-Zumar: 71].

The third aspect: the pronoun in His saying ﴿and indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ refers to the Lord of man mentioned in His saying ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾. In that case, there is no difficulty in the verse. However, its reference to man is more apparent, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿and indeed he is, in his love of wealth, intense﴾ [Al-'Adiyat: 8].

And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 100, verse 7:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, he is, concerning that, a witness﴾.

There is a difference of opinion regarding the referent of the pronoun in "wa-innahu" (and indeed he). It has been said that it refers to man (al-insan), and our Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him and us, preferred this view in dispelling the appearance of inconsistency, citing His saying after it: ﴿And indeed, he is, in his love of wealth, intense﴾.

It has also been said that it refers to the Lord of man (rabb al-insan).

Al-Qurtubi chose this view and gave it precedence.

All the commentators mention the difference of opinion, and you have come to know the preferred view among them. Accordingly, if the pronoun refers to the Lord of man, there is no difficulty in the verse. If it refers to man, there is a difficulty, which our Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him and us, raised in dispelling the appearance of inconsistency, and he answered it.

It is this: there are texts indicating that he (man) denies that, and that he loves wealth intensely, and similar things.

Among the answers to it: that his witnessing is by the tongue of his state (lisan al-hal), i.e., by the condition of his conduct rather than by his speech.

Some commentators have cited witnessing by the tongue of speech (lisan al-maqal) in His saying: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves with disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17]. However, this witnessing with disbelief is polytheism (al-shirk). And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, he is, in his love of wealth, intense﴾.

"Good" (al-khayr) is general, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾.

However, here it is specific to wealth. It is thus of the general term that is intended in a specific sense, by restricting the general to some of its individuals, since wealth is one individual of "good," like His saying: ﴿if he leaves behind some good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], meaning wealth, because the doing of good accompanies a person and does not leave him.

On this there are two interpretations. The first: ﴿and indeed, he is, in his love of good﴾, i.e., because of his love of good, ﴿intense﴾, i.e., stingy, extremely miserly.

As it has been said:

"I see death selecting the noble and choosing the choicest wealth of the immoderate, overbearing one."

That is, "intense" here means extremely miserly according to the reading of this line.

The second interpretation: "and indeed, he is intensely loving of wealth." Both were stated by Ibn Kathir.

He said: "Both are correct, and in reality the second includes the first."

What supports the second interpretation is His saying: ﴿and you devour the heritage with greedy devouring﴾ ﴿and you love wealth with abundant love﴾.

We have said that the second includes the first, because whoever loves wealth with abundant love, his love will drive him to miserliness.

In this text there is a censure of the love of wealth, which is an innate disposition in man, except for one whom Islam has refined. However, the blame falls upon the excessive love that carries its possessor to the loss of rights or the transgression of limits.

This verse and what precedes it were revealed concerning the disbelievers, as we have already cited the words of the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, in his dictation.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 100, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾.

Al-ba'tharah (ba'thara, the scattering and spreading out) is al-intithar (dispersal).

Al-Zamakhshari said: this word is derived from two roots: al-ba'th (raising, sending forth) and al-nath'r (scattering).

So al-ba'th is their coming out alive.

And al-nathr is al-intishar (spreading out), like the scattering of grain; it indicates their being raised up dispersed.

(p-68) Exalted is He has explicitly stated this meaning in His saying: ﴿And when the graves are scattered forth﴾ [al-Infitar: 4], meaning: whoever is in them is scattered forth.

And His saying: ﴿On the Day they will come out from the graves swiftly﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43].

And His saying: ﴿As if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7].

And His saying: ﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 100, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what is in the breasts is brought out﴾.

It has been said: "hussila" means "ubriza" (was brought forth/exposed). This is what Ibn 'Abbas said.

It has also been said: it distinguishes the good from the evil.

Al-hasil (that which remains) of everything is what is left over.

Labid said:

Every man will one day know his striving, when the remainders are gathered before God.

The intended meaning of "what is in the breasts" is the deeds, and this is like His saying: ﴿On the Day when secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 9].

The breasts are specified here, although what is meant is the hearts, because they are the locus of action (manat al-'amal) and the seat of intention (ma'qid al-niyyah).

Creed and the soundness of all deeds revolve around intention, as in the hadith: "Actions are only by intentions" (innama al-a'mal bi'l-niyyat), and the hadith: "Verily, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound," and so on.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: He singled out the heart for mention because it is the place of the foundations of actions.

For this reason He mentioned it in the context of blame: ﴿For indeed, its heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], and in the context of praise: ﴿Their hearts tremble﴾ [al-Anfal: 2].

What he said is supported by His saying: ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 89].

And His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74].

And He said: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften﴾ [al-Zumar: 23].

And His saying: ﴿Surely, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28], and similar verses.

Among what indicates that the intended meaning of "the breasts" is what is within them is the heart, is His saying: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded﴾ [al-Hajj: 46].

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: He mentioned the breasts so as to include both good and evil, since the heart is the locus of faith.

The breast is also the locus of whisperings, according to His saying: ﴿The one who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 5].

Although this is a sound view, the locus of whisperings is also the heart, so it returns to the first meaning. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 100, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, their Lord, that Day, is fully Acquainted with them.﴾

Mentioning the time-frame here ("that Day") gives the impression that the description is restricted to that Day, although He, glorified is He, is Acquainted with them at every moment, on that Day and before that Day. Rather, on that Day He brings to light what had been hidden. He, glorified is He, knows the secret and what is even more hidden, and nothing whatsoever is concealed from Him.

However, the mention of the time-frame here serves as a warning, together with the description "Khabir" (Acquainted), which is more specific than "'Alim" (Knowing), as in His saying: ﴿The All-Knowing, the Acquainted, informed me﴾ [al-Tahrim: 3].
